steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on gender bias in large language models across multiple languages. It should motivate why bias in LLMs matters, point out gaps in earlier gender bias evaluations, and introduce our multi-dimensional measurements, our multilingual experiments and the main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs are spreading into socially influential areas, so bias matters
- Prior gender bias work and its gaps (English-only, single task, single dimension)
- Why multiple languages matter
- Our approach: three measurements of gender bias
- Experiments across languages and the main conclusions
- Outlook and code release

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
LLMs are developing quickly and are being applied to many areas, notably dialogue systems and creative writing, so these models are no longer just tools for daily convenience. LLMs are more and more common in social-influencing domains such as education and the technology industry, and they play a more and more important role in social influence. In this context the existence of bias is harmful, because the social influence of LLMs can further promote the underlying legal and ethical implications.

Many previous studies have found gender bias in NLP models. For gender bias in LLMs, previous works usually focus on certain tasks in the English context and use single-dimensional evaluation methods for gender bias. This neglects the fact that LLMs generally get different types of instructions in different use circumstances, and the gender bias can show up in different aspects. Since LLM users have diverse language backgrounds and the LLMs themselves have strong capabilities in multilingual reasoning, it is important to emphasize the various language features and cultural influences that affect how gender bias occurs in different languages. Different languages may have different degrees of gender bias in LLM generations, and understanding this is essential for acknowledging and mitigating these biases in LLMs and making sure they are more equitable and culturally aware in the wide range of applications.

- Our approach
  - emphasize role of conversations by LLMs; gender bias in different dimensions
  - three quantitative evaluation measurements -> three-dimensional aspects
- Experiments
  - six languages, range of state-of-the-art LLMs, e.g. GPT-3/4
  - compare levels and nuances of bias across languages
  - lexicon and sentiment aspects; diverse instructions influence bias differently
  - conclusions:
    1. co-occurrence probability between descriptive words and genders
    2. prediction of gender roles given a type of personal description
    3. divergence of underlying sentiment tendency of dialogue topics between gender pairs
- Wrap-up
  - bias from different aspects; future de-biasing of LLM-generated text with gender info
  - code at https://anonymous.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
LLMs are developing quickly and are being applied to many areas, notably dialogue systems and creative writing, so these models are no longer just tools for daily convenience. LLMs are more and more common in social-influencing domains such as education and the technology industry, and they play a more and more important role in social influence. In this context the existence of bias is harmful, because the social influence of LLMs can further promote the underlying legal and ethical implications.

Many previous studies have found gender bias in NLP models. For gender bias in LLMs, previous works usually focus on certain tasks in the English context and use single-dimensional evaluation methods for gender bias. This neglects the fact that LLMs generally get different types of instructions in different use circumstances, and the gender bias can show up in different aspects. Since LLM users have diverse language backgrounds and the LLMs themselves have strong capabilities in multilingual reasoning, it is important to emphasize the various language features and cultural influences that affect how gender bias occurs in different languages. Different languages may have different degrees of gender bias in LLM generations, and understanding this is essential for acknowledging and mitigating these biases in LLMs and making sure they are more equitable and culturally aware in the wide range of applications.

To address these limitations of gender bias evaluation in LLMs, our study emphasizes the big role of conversations done by LLMs and explores gender bias in different dimensions. In particular we present three quantitative evaluation measurements for gender bias in LLMs, which can show three-dimensional aspects of gender bias.

Using these measurements, we do experiments in six different languages with a range of state-of-the-art LLMs, such as GPT-3/4, which lets us compare the levels and nuances of gender bias across these languages. Our approaches make it possible to do a comprehensive analysis of both lexicon and sentiment aspects of gender bias across different languages, and they give insights into the fact that diverse instructions may influence gender biases in LLM generations in different ways. The main results can be put into the following conclusions:

- 1. Gender bias appears in the co-occurrence probability between certain descriptive words and genders.

- 2. Gender bias appears in the prediction of gender roles given a certain type of personal description.

- 3. Gender bias appears in the divergence of the underlying sentiment tendency shown by the dialogue topics between different gender pairs.

These findings show the gender bias in LLM generations from different aspects and shed light on future work to de-bias LLM-generated text that contains gender information. The code will be released at https://anonymous.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the rapid development of LLMs applied to numerous areas, notably dialogue systems [1] and creative writing [2], these models have gone beyond their role as mere tools for daily convenience. LLMs have become increasingly prevalent in various social-influencing domains such as education [3,4] and the technology industry [5], playing an increasingly important role in social influence. The existence of bias is harmful in such a context, as the social influence of LLMs can further promote the underlying legal and ethical implications [6,7].

Many previous studies have identified gender bias in NLP models [8,9]. For gender bias in LLMs, previous works usually focus on certain tasks in the English context and use single-dimensional evaluation methods [10,11], neglecting the fact that LLMs generally receive different types of instructions for different use circumstances, where gender bias can be reflected in different aspects. Considering the diverse language backgrounds of LLM users and the strong multilingual reasoning capabilities of the LLMs themselves [12,13,14,15], it is important to emphasize the various language features and cultural influences that affect how gender bias occurs in different languages. Different languages may exhibit different degrees of gender bias in LLM generations; such an understanding is essential for acknowledging and mitigating these biases, ensuring LLMs are more equitable and culturally aware across the wide range of applications.

To address these limitations of gender bias evaluation in LLMs, our study emphasizes the substantial role of conversations undertaken by LLMs and explores gender bias in different dimensions. In particular, we present three quantitative evaluation measurements for gender bias in LLMs, which reveal three-dimensional aspects of gender bias.

Based on the proposed measurements, we conduct experiments in six different languages using a range of state-of-the-art LLMs, such as GPT-3/4 [16], allowing us to compare the levels and nuances of gender bias across these languages. Our approaches facilitate a comprehensive analysis of both the lexicon and sentiment aspects of gender bias across different languages, providing insights into how diverse instructions may influence gender biases in LLM generations in different ways. The main results of our exploration fall into the following conclusions:

- 1. Gender bias appears in the co-occurrence probability between certain descriptive words and genders.

- 2. Gender bias appears in the prediction of gender roles given a certain type of personal description.

- 3. Gender bias appears in the divergence of the underlying sentiment tendency reflected by the dialogue topics between different gender pairs.

These findings reveal gender bias in LLM generations from different aspects and shed light on future work to de-bias LLM-generated text containing gender information. The code will be released at https://anonymous.
